strengths: Principled and clearly motivated framework: the paper correctly identifies the tension between scalable coarse-grained (CG) surrogates (biased, no reweighting) and atomistic Boltzmann Generators (exact but poorly scalable), and proposes a clean reconciliation by targeting the CG marginal p(R) with a learned PMF as the importance-sampling target energy. The conceptual unification of reduced-order modeling with rigorous reweighting is a genuinely useful idea.

Good methodological hygiene in the reference choice: unlike much prior BG work that treats implicit solvent as ground truth, the authors use explicit-solvent MD as the reference and treat implicit-solvent models (OBC1/OBC2) as baselines (Tab. 2). This is a meaningful improvement in evaluation practice.

The simulation-free evaluation of learned PMFs (§4.3, Fig. 5, Fig. 9) is a nice, practically useful byproduct: reusing a single set of flow samples and weights to benchmark candidate PMFs without additional MD. This is a concrete, transferable contribution.

The paper is well written and reasonably reproducible: appendices give detailed architectures (§C.1, §D.1), training configurations (§C.2, §D.2), simulation parameters (Tab. 3), hardware/software (§E), and pseudocode (Algorithms 1–3). Propositions 1–3 are provided with proofs in §A.1–A.2.

Ablations are performed in good faith: weight-clipping sensitivity (Fig. 12, Tab. 6), the effect of CG resolution (Heavy Atom vs Core Beta), and the biased-vs-unbiased data regimes are all explored, and the limitations section candidly identifies the reliance on predefined CVs and the accuracy loss at coarser resolutions.
weaknesses: The central claim of scalability to 'larger molecular systems' is not substantiated. The only systems evaluated are the 2-D Müller–Brown toy potential and alanine dipeptide (22 atoms). Alanine dipeptide is the smallest standard test case in this literature; demonstrating 'highly reduced representations' of solvent-mediated effects on a single capped residue does not support the abstract's claim of 'a scalable pathway for the unbiased sampling of larger molecular systems.' No larger peptide, protein, or multi-residue system is shown.

The claimed 'exactness' / 'asymptotically correct statistics' is undercut by the weight-clipping step. Tab. 6 shows that without clipping (0%) the estimator degenerates (ESS ~ 0, PMF error 8–262), while the reported results all use 1% clipping, which by the authors' own admission (Fig. 12) introduces bias. Thus the method's headline exactness property holds only in an idealized regime that the authors do not use, and the reported numbers come from a biased estimator. The paper should be explicit that reported metrics are not asymptotically unbiased.

Exactness is only with respect to the CG marginal p(R), not the atomistic distribution. Because the PMF integrates out eliminated degrees of freedom, observables depending on those degrees of freedom cannot be recovered. The paper acknowledges backmapping as related work but does not implement or evaluate it, so the practical scope of 'unbiased equilibrium sampling' is limited to CG-observable quantities. This significantly narrows the significance relative to the abstract's framing.

The core PMF-learning machinery is not original: Propositions 2 and 3 (conditional invariance of the fiber distribution under CG bias, and equivalence of the ESFM optimum to standard force matching) are attributed to Chen et al. (2026). The novelty is therefore the combination of existing components (CNF/flow matching, ESFM, PMF-as-energy, importance sampling) rather than any new theoretical result, which makes the contribution incremental.

The efficiency comparison is not apples-to-apples. Tab. 1's 'All Atom' baseline generates only solute coordinates and explicitly omits solvent ('generating full configurations with explicit solvent... is computationally infeasible'), so the reported speedups conflate reduced dimensionality with omission of the solvent degrees of freedom. The comparison with prior BG timings (Tab. 4) also mixes in numbers taken from other papers († entries) without a controlled benchmark.

Effective sample sizes are low (ESS ≈ 0.19–0.25 in Tab. 2), meaning only ~1/5 to ~1/4 of samples effectively contribute. This is not discussed as a limitation of the framework's practicality, and no comparison to an atomistic BG baseline (same system, reweighted) is provided to situate these numbers.

Prop. 1's bound relies on a Log-Sobolev inequality, which the authors themselves note is a strong assumption for multimodal PMFs (as in alanine dipeptide). It is therefore a weak theoretical motivation rather than a guarantee, and it does not address the bias introduced by the clipping actually used in practice.

strengths: Principled and conceptually clean combination of Boltzmann Generators with coarse-graining: performing both the generative proposal and the importance reweighting in CG space with a learned PMF as the target energy is a sensible way to address the scalability-vs-exactness tradeoff.

Using explicit solvent simulations as the reference (and treating implicit solvent models as baselines) is a genuine methodological improvement over much prior BG work, which is fundamentally limited by implicit-solvent approximation error.

Learning the PMF via enhanced-sampling force matching (ESFM) from rapidly converged biased data is a reasonable route to avoid the cost of long unbiased trajectories, and Propositions 2–3 correctly justify the fiber-invariance argument.

The paper is largely reproducible: architectures (Graph Transformer flow, MACE PMF), hyperparameters, simulation protocols (GROMACS/OpenMM, WT-MetaD, TIP3P, force fields), software, and compute are documented in detail in the appendices and algorithms.
The simulation-free PMF evaluation paradigm is a practically useful byproduct that could serve as a diagnostic tool for CG potentials.
Limitations and the weight-clipping ablation are reported honestly rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The central 'asymptotically exact / unbiased' claim is contradicted by the authors' own ablation. Without weight clipping, ESS collapses to ~0.0000–0.0001 and JS/PMF errors explode (Table 6: JS 0.0075→0.2364, PMF 0.2493→8.3338). The method therefore only 'works' because the top 1% of weights are discarded — a bias-inducing operation. Raw importance reweighting (the core mechanism inherited from BGs) essentially fails, so the headline of exact/unbiased statistics is unsupported.

The scalability claim — the primary motivation — is not demonstrated. Evaluation is restricted to the 2D Müller–Brown toy and alanine dipeptide (22 atoms), the smallest possible molecular test cases. No larger or genuinely complex system is attempted, so the 'scalable pathway for unbiased sampling of larger molecular systems' remains an assertion.

Novelty is limited and partly inherited. All ingredients exist (Boltzmann Generators, flow matching, variational force matching, PMF learning), and Propositions 2 and 3 are explicitly attributed to prior work (Chen et al., 2026). The novel claim ('first BG using an MLP as target energy for importance sampling') is narrow, and the framework is essentially an assembly of known components.

Reweighting does not improve the primary reported accuracy metric in key settings. For Heavy Atom trained on unbiased data, the JS divergence is 0.0074 for the raw proposal vs. 0.0075 after reweighting — i.e., no improvement (or slightly worse). Gains are confined to PMF error, which weakens the demonstration that reweighting is necessary or beneficial.

The computational-cost comparison is not apples-to-apples. The 'All Atom' baseline generates only solute coordinates (explicit solvent is acknowledged as infeasible), and comparisons to ECNF++/SBG/DiT-CNF/FALCON are timing-only values copied from Rehman et al. (2025) with no head-to-head accuracy comparison against an atomistic BG on the same system.

The data bottleneck is shifted rather than removed. The PMF requires enhanced-sampling simulations with pre-defined collective variables (the backbone dihedrals), which are trivially known for alanine dipeptide but nontrivial for complex systems — exactly the regime the paper claims to enable. This undercuts the scalability argument even though it is acknowledged in the limitations.

Theoretical motivation is weak: Proposition 1 relies on a Log-Sobolev inequality that the paper itself concedes is a strong assumption violated by multimodal PMFs, so the bound provides limited practical justification for the force-matching objective.

Reported metrics are narrow and somewhat ambiguous. JS/PMF errors are computed only on projected dihedral observables, and the 'reference' derives from finite (500 ns) MD; the reported uncertainties (e.g., ±0.0001) appear to reflect sampling of reweighted points rather than systematic convergence of the reference.

strengths: Principled and clean framework: unifying coarse-grained reduced-order modeling with importance sampling by using a learned potential of mean force (PMF) as the target energy for reweighting is a sensible and well-motivated extension of Boltzmann Generators to CG space.

Using enhanced-sampling force matching (ESFM) to learn the PMF from rapidly converged biased data directly addresses the real circular-dependency problem in CG surrogate training, where unbiased equilibrium data is itself the bottleneck.

The theoretical components are sound: Proposition 1 (an LSI-based bound linking KL divergence to expected squared force error) and Proposition 2 (fiber/conditional-distribution invariance under CG-only bias) are correctly derived in the appendix, and they meaningfully motivate the training objective.

The paper is honest and informative about weight clipping (Table 6, Fig. 12), showing that un-clipped reweighting collapses to near-zero ESS and that a conservative 1% clipping is needed to balance the bias-variance tradeoff.

The comparison against implicit solvent baselines (OBC1/OBC2) is a valuable framing, showing that PMFs learned from explicit solvent can outperform implicit-solvent references, which is a genuine limitation of prior atomistic BG work.
The simulation-free PMF evaluation paradigm (Section 4.3) is a useful practical side contribution for rapidly validating learned CG potentials without additional MD.
Reproducibility documentation is strong: architectures, hyperparameters, dataset construction, compute infrastructure, and algorithms are described in detail across appendices.
weaknesses: The 'exactness/unbiasedness' framing is overstated. Reweighting targets p_eta(R) ∝ exp(-β U_eta(R)), not the true marginal p(R); the systematic error of the learned PMF is not corrected by importance sampling. The abstract's 'unbiased sampling of larger molecular systems' and the claim of inheriting the 'exactness of importance sampling' are therefore misleading. The paper hedges in Section 3.3 but not in the abstract/intro.

The scalability claim is not substantiated by the experiments, which are limited to a 2D Müller-Brown toy and alanine dipeptide (22 atoms) — one of the smallest molecular benchmarks. No demonstration on a genuinely large or solvent-explicit full system is provided, so the central 'scalable pathway' claim remains aspirational.

Limited novelty. The PMF-learning component (ESFM) is taken from prior work (Chen et al., 2026); the contribution is essentially the combination of an existing CG force-matching scheme with flow-based reweighting. The claim of being the 'first BG formulation that incorporates MLPs as the target energy for importance sampling' is debatable given related energy-based / learned-potential reweighting work.

Weight clipping is required for numerical stability (un-clipped reweighting gives ESS ≈ 0 and huge JS/PMF errors) and introduces an explicit bias, which sits uneasily with the unbiasedness claim; ESS after clipping is still low (~0.19-0.25).

No comparison of the PMF learning against alternative CG potential learning methods (e.g., relative entropy minimization), so the specific advantage of ESFM over existing alternatives is not established.

The all-atom efficiency baseline only generates solute coordinates without solvent, so the timing comparison (Table 1/4) is not apples-to-apples with the explicit-solvent reference; this is acknowledged but still weakens the efficiency argument.
Evaluation is restricted to a single molecular system; robustness across systems, mappings, and temperatures is not demonstrated, and no code release is mentioned to support reproducibility.

strengths: Introduces CG-BGs, a useful framework that combines coarse-graining, exact-likelihood flow models, and importance reweighting with a learned potential of mean force (PMF), addressing scalability limits of atomistic Boltzmann Generators and the bias of reweighting-free Boltzmann Emulators.

Shows how enhanced-sampling force matching (ESFM) can learn the PMF from rapidly converged biased trajectories rather than long unbiased equilibrium data, with Propositions 2 and 3 giving a clear invariance and optimum argument.

Provides a theoretical link between force-matching error and KL divergence via a Log-Sobolev inequality (Proposition 1), which, although based on strong assumptions, motivates the use of force matching for distributional accuracy.

Demonstrates on Müller-Brown and alanine peptide systems that reweighting corrects imperfect flow proposals and recovers equilibrium dihedral free-energy profiles, including from biased WT-MetaD data.

Reports that reweighted CG-BGs can outperform implicit-solvent MD baselines, supporting the claim that PMFs learned from explicit-solvent data capture solvent-mediated effects without explicit solvent during sampling.

Proposes a simulation-free PMF evaluation idea: once a flow proposal is trained, multiple learned potentials can be compared by reweighting a single sample set, which is practically useful for CG model assessment.
Includes detailed appendices with architectures, training hyperparameters, datasets, algorithms, compute infrastructure, and additional results, making the experimental setup largely traceable.
The limitations section honestly identifies the reliance on predefined collective variables and suggests uncertainty quantification and CV discovery as future directions.
weaknesses: The central 'asymptotically exact' framing is too strong in practice: exactness holds only for the learned PMF p_eta under idealized assumptions, while finite data, model error, and weight clipping introduce uncontrolled bias relative to the true marginal p(R).

Weight clipping discards the top 1% of importance weights, which explicitly breaks unbiasedness. The ablations show that without clipping, metrics degrade severely due to weight degeneracy, so the method relies on a biased estimator for stable results; this bias is not theoretically controlled and is not discussed in the main limitations.

For tripeptide and hexapeptide, WT-MetaD biases only a selected dihedral pair, so the learned PMF may not be globally accurate. Evaluation is then focused on that same biased dihedral pair, creating a risk that reported accuracy is favorable to the chosen setup.

Evaluation is limited to small peptide systems (up to 72 atoms) and a few observables. The abstract and conclusion claim a practical route toward larger systems, but the experiments do not substantiate scalability beyond small alanine peptides.

Computational cost comparisons are incomplete: the main tables report flow training/inference and sometimes PMF training, but exclude the substantial cost of generating biased/unbiased MD data. Comparisons with atomistic BGs also use numbers from prior work with different hardware, batch sizes, and implementations.

The comparison to atomistic BGs is indirect and somewhat uneven: atomistic BGs are trained with implicit-solvent energies, while CG-BGs reweight with a learned explicit-solvent PMF. This conflates the benefit of the target energy with the benefit of the CG-BG framework.

Several technical details are underspecified. For example, the projected force F_proj is not explicitly defined, and Proposition 1 does not connect the training objective under the biased data distribution to the expected force error under p_eta appearing in the bound.
The Log-Sobolev inequality assumption in Proposition 1 is strong for multimodal PMFs, as the authors acknowledge, but its practical relevance for the reported systems is not empirically tested.

No code or data release is mentioned, and reproducing the full pipeline requires external MD simulations (GROMACS/OpenMM/PLUMED) plus JAX/chemtrain setups, limiting reproducibility despite the detailed appendices.

The language around unbiasedness should be more careful: after weight clipping and with an approximate PMF, estimates are not asymptotically exact for the true equilibrium distribution, and this distinction should be emphasized in the abstract and main text.

strengths: Coherent, well-motivated framework that combines coarse-grained modeling with Boltzmann-Generator-style importance reweighting to attack a genuine scalability problem in equilibrium sampling.

The use of enhanced-sampling force matching (ESFM) to learn the PMF from rapidly converged biased trajectories is practically valuable and the invariance argument (Proposition 2) is correctly exploited; it removes reliance on long unbiased MD and offers a correction path for existing CG Boltzmann Emulators.

End-to-end empirical demonstrations on alanine di-/-tri-/-hexapeptide (and Müller-Brown) with both unbiased and WT-MetaD training data show that reweighting recovers dihedral free-energy profiles and outperforms implicit-solvent baselines; the appendices provide detailed algorithms, architectures, hyperparameters, and a weight-clipping ablation.
The limitations section is honest, and the 'simulation-free PMF benchmarking' idea (reusing a fixed proposal to compare multiple candidate potentials) is a genuinely useful practical observation.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: training/sampling algorithms are given explicitly, software (JAX/Diffrax/Flax/chemtrain) and hardware are listed, and dataset construction is documented.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'asymptotically correct/unbiased' sampling is not supported. The importance weights target exp(-βU_η)/q_θ, i.e., the *learned* PMF, not the true marginal p*(R). Any correctness with respect to the true Boltzmann distribution depends entirely on PMF accuracy, with no reweighting guarantee against a wrong potential. This is materially weaker than atomistic BGs (whose target is the true energy), yet the abstract, introduction, and contribution list present it as rigorous/asymptotically exact ('enabling asymptotically correct equilibrium sampling', 'correction mechanism for Boltzmann Emulators') without that caveat.

Weight clipping (discarding the top 1% highest-weight samples) is an ad hoc, bias-inducing procedure that directly undercuts the unbiasedness claim, and the reported ESS/JS/PMF numbers are computed *after* clipping. The ablation (Tables 7-9) shows metrics are highly sensitive to the clipping ratio (e.g., hexapeptide ESS collapses to ~2e-4 at 0% clip, and the chosen 1% clip sometimes *worsens* PMF vs 0%), so results rest on an unprincipled threshold.

Novelty is incremental. The PMF-learning machinery (ESFM) and Propositions 2-3 are taken from prior work (Chen et al., 2026); Proposition 1 is a standard LSI-based bound that the authors themselves flag as relying on strong assumptions for multimodal PMFs. The core contribution reduces to combining existing BG reweighting with existing PMF learning, and the 'simulation-free evaluation' section is essentially a restatement of importance sampling.

Evaluation is weak relative to the claims. Metrics (JS divergence, PMF error) are computed only on 1D/2D dihedral projections, systems are small (≤72 atoms), and the paper's central scalability motivation to 'larger molecular systems' is never demonstrated. The strongest reduction claim is also the weakest result: the Core Beta hexapeptide case has ESS ≈ 0.12 and the largest PMF error, which does not support 'highly reduced representations' capturing solvent-mediated effects robustly.

Baseline comparisons are not apples-to-apples and appear constructed to favor the method. Comparing explicit-solvent-trained CG-BGs against implicit-solvent MD is expected to win and mostly demonstrates that implicit solvent is inaccurate rather than that the method is superior; atomistic BG numbers (TarFlow, ECNF++, e.g., ESS 0.0034) are imported from the literature under different training conditions and live in a different coordinate space, making the 'outperforms atomistic BGs' claim unsupported.

Presentation/reproducibility quality issues: the reference list contains numerous citation-year mismatches (e.g., 'Kidger (1965)', 'Kish and Su (1965)', 'Hutchinson et al. (2022)', 'Chen, R. T., Rubanova' vs. cited 'Chen et al., 2018') and multiple future-dated arXiv IDs, suggesting careless preparation that hinders verification.

The learned PMF is never validated directly against an independent reference PMF (e.g., umbrella-sampling/WHAM); validation is only end-to-end through reweighted observables, so a systematic PMF bias could be partially masked by the same reweighting being used to evaluate it.

strengths: The paper presents a clean and well-motivated framework (CG-BGs) that combines normalizing flows over coarse-grained coordinates with a learned PMF used as the target energy for importance sampling. The conceptual framing—reduced-order generative modeling with reweighting in CG space—is sensible and addresses a real scalability bottleneck in Boltzmann Generators.

The use of enhanced sampling force matching (ESFM) to learn the PMF from rapidly converged biased trajectories is a practical and valuable design choice. The fiber-invariance argument (Proposition 2) correctly justifies that the regression target is unchanged under CG biasing, and the empirical results support faster convergence relative to requiring long unbiased MD.

The experimental work is substantial and reasonably thorough: it spans the analytically tractable Müller–Brown potential and three alanine peptides (di-/tri-/hexapeptide), multiple CG mappings, biased vs. unbiased training regimes, and includes ablation studies (weight clipping ratio), free energy profiles for phi/psi, Ramachandran plots, and bond-length distributions in the appendix.

The comparison against implicit solvent baselines and atomistic BGs (TarFlow, ECNF++) is informative, and the finding that reweighted CG-BGs can outperform implicit-solvent-limited atomistic BGs is a meaningful, concrete result. The simulation-free PMF evaluation idea (reusing one flow proposal to compare multiple candidate PMFs) is a nice practical contribution.

The paper is well written, the notation is consistent, and reproducibility is reasonably supported: architectures, training configurations, algorithms, compute infrastructure, and dataset details are all provided.
Limitations (predefined CVs, PMF approximation bias) are discussed honestly rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'asymptotically correct' equilibrium sampling is conditional and somewhat overstated. The estimator targets the distribution induced by the *learned* PMF U_eta, not the true atomistic marginal, so correctness holds only in the idealized limit where U_eta is exact. The authors acknowledge 'approximation bias' but the framing throughout emphasizes asymptotic exactness, which could mislead readers about the guarantees.

The weight-clipping strategy (discarding the top 1% of weights) introduces bias into an estimator whose main selling point is unbiasedness. The ablation (Tabs. 7–9) shows that without clipping, ESS collapses dramatically (e.g., 0.0002 for hexapeptide), meaning the reported quality relies on a biased post-hoc correction. This tension between the unbiasedness claim and the practical dependence on clipping is not fully reconciled.

Novelty is largely integrative: the components (Boltzmann Generators, coarse-graining, ESFM from Chen et al. 2026, flow matching) all exist, and the contribution is their combination. The ESFM machinery is not new to this work. The incremental nature is acceptable but reduces the strength of the contribution.

The scalability claim is not substantiated by the experiments. The largest system studied is alanine hexapeptide (72 atoms), which is still small; no demonstration on genuinely large molecular systems is provided, yet 'scalable pathway for sampling high-dimensional molecular systems' is a headline claim.

CG-BGs only sample CG coordinates, and backmapping to atomistic configurations is not addressed. Many observables of interest are atomistic, so the practical reach of the framework is narrower than the framing suggests, and the comparison to 'atomistic BGs' is not fully apples-to-apples (CG-BG never produces full atomistic samples).

The theoretical support is thin for the actual setting: Proposition 1 relies on a Logarithmic Sobolev Inequality, which the authors themselves note is a 'strong assumption' that generally fails for the multimodal PMFs encountered in practice, so the bound provides little practical guidance.

Evaluation metrics are relatively narrow (JS divergence and PMF error on a few dihedral angles, plus ESS). These are standard, but the evidence that the method recovers *global* equilibrium statistics—especially given biasing applied only to a single dihedral pair for the larger peptides—is limited; the authors acknowledge that convergence is primarily enforced along the targeted CVs.

The 'all atom' computational baseline generates only solute coordinates, so the headline efficiency comparison against atomistic BGs is not on equal footing (acknowledged, but it weakens the cost claim).
